 New Federal Earnings Rule: What Students Need to Know
 October 26, 2026 
 Nine minutes 
 Share 
 By Catherine Brown, Senior Director, Policy and Advocacy; and Bill DeBaun, Senior Director, Data and Strategic Initiatives 
 Share 
 Copy Link 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 X 
 Facebook 
 For the first time this year, every college program (“major”) that accepts federal student aid must show that its graduates earn more than people who never enrolled. The rule matters for the students NCAN members serve because it could limit the postsecondary programs that are available to them, but its reach is narrow, and most programs will clear it easily. It’s also worth noting that the programs that don't meet this new standard are those where the students will leave the program earning less than they would have had they never gone in the first place.   
 The US Department of Education (ED) finalized this test on July 1, 2026. It implements the "Do No Harm" earnings standard Congress enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in July 2025, and it replaces the prior gainful employment and financial value transparency rules with a new Student Tuition and Transparency System (STATS).  
 We know that there are concerns that the rule will foreclose access to programs that offer societal value, like social workers, clergy members, or early childhood educators, but the rule was designed to protect students from taking out loans to attend programs that won’t offer economic returns.   
 Let’s dive in.  
 What the Rule Does 
 The test: Each program (e.g. “major”) will be measured on the median earnings of its completers four years after they finish:  
 Undergraduate programs, including certificates, must exceed the median earnings of working adults ages 25–34 with only a high school diploma in the college's state or nationally if more than half of students come from outside the state. 
 Graduate programs must beat the median earnings of working adults ages 25–34 with only a bachelor's degree. 
 Reminder: Median earnings is the middle value: if you lined up everyone in the group from lowest to highest earnings, it’s the amount earned by the person in the middle. Half earn less, and half earn more. Unlike an average, the median isn’t skewed by a few very high earners, so it gives a better sense of what a typical person makes.  
 The consequences:   
 A program that fails to meet the standard in two of three consecutive years loses access to federal Direct Loans. An entire institution can lose all Title IV aid, including Pell Grants, if more than half of its aided students or aid dollars are tied to failing programs. Note that this is a high bar that most colleges and universities are highly unlikely to hit.   
 Trade schools and proprietary schools with a limited number of offerings are at greater risk.   
 Colleges will receive a warning after a program fails the test once. They will then be able to stop offering federal student loans for that program, close the program and stop offering it to students, or wait for future results.  
 The timeline. Colleges had to submit their first STATS data by October 1, 2026. The Department will run the first earnings test in early 2027. The earliest any program could lose loan access is the 2028–29 award year.  
 New disclosures for students. Colleges must warn current and prospective students when a program is at risk of losing federal student aid. They must also tell Pell recipients how much lifetime Pell eligibility they have left each time a grant is disbursed.  
 There are some weaknesses in the rule that may make it not a strong test of a program’s quality and likely impact on a student’s earnings trajectory:   
 First, the rule does not count student debt, so a program can pass the earnings test even if the average borrower has taken out an unmanageable level of debt to afford to attend. The rule used to be a debt-to-earnings ratio.   
 Second, only students who complete the program count towards the test. Students who drop out, often with debt, are not included, which will have the effect of biasing the earnings data upwards.   
 Third, the Pell Grant can keep flowing to schools with failing programs. A college can give up federal loans for a failing program and keep its Pell-eligibility, resulting in students spending their limited lifetime Pell-eligibility on programs that will not benefit them financially.   
 Lastly, the final rule delays consequences for programs tied to about 20 tipped occupations, mainly cosmetology , barbering, and massage therapy, some of the most cited programs likely to fail the test.  
 This Rule’s Estimated Impact 
 According to a new PEER Center analysis by Jordan Matsudaira, Kristen Allen, and Clare McCann, released October 14, the rule will impact only about 2.5% of students receiving federal student aid. Using ED data from the federal rulemaking, they found:  
 Undergraduate certificates and for-profit colleges will be the most heavily impacted. Undergraduate certificates make up 10% of Title IV (postsecondary institutions awarding federal student aid) enrollment, but these programs comprise 63% of the enrollment in programs projected to fail the rule. Cosmetology, allied health, and medical administration stand out. About 13.7% of students attending for-profit colleges (roughly 281,000) are in failing programs, compared with 0.8% at public colleges and 2.3% at private nonprofits.  
 Most colleges have no failing programs at all . That includes nearly 70% of community colleges, 75% of public four-year colleges, and 84% of private nonprofit four-year colleges. 
 Many people are worried that the rule will penalize fields that serve their communities but pay modestly, such as teaching, social work, ministry, and music. At the undergraduate level, the risk is small. ED projects that programs enrolling less than 1% of bachelor's students will fail. It’s also important to note that this rule does not preclude students from enrolling in postsecondary programs in these fields of study. If anything, it simply narrows their options to programs that have produced better earnings, on average. It also speaks to the earnings premium observed for decades from bachelor’s degree attainment. 
 Graduate programs may be more exposed, but they are compared to the earnings of people with bachelor’s degree who are working in the same field and state . Therefore, a master's degree in social work or education is not measured against an engineering undergraduate degree. Even so, PEER finds higher failure rates in graduate programs in mental and social health services, largely at online-focused institutions. 
 Religious programs received relief in the final rule; the Department says its exemptions for programs that do not use federal loans will shield about 600 of them from consequences, according to the Council for Higher Education Accreditation (CHEA). “The final rule will reduce the consequences by roughly half on students and Title IV program funds disbursed to religious programs relative to the current regulations,” continues the CHEA analysis. 
 Arts programs such as music performance are harder to predict because performers' freelance income can be uneven four years out, so advisors should look up specific programs rather than assume a field is safe or at risk. 
 Early childhood education (ECE) programs could be at risk, according to an analysis from New America. More data is needed to assess the impact of the rule on this occupation and programs. ED refused to carve ECE programs out despite receiving a lot of comments requesting that change. 
 Tools for Students and Advisors   
 It’s important for college access advisors to understand this rule, what it does, and most importantly what it doesn’t do. For most students, fears about their program losing access to Direct Loans are probably misplaced. More broadly, advisors, students, and families should know where to find information about how to assess, prior to enrolling, the quality of a program and its likely impact on student earnings. These free tools let advisors check out a specific program before a student commits. 
  Tool 
  What it shows 
  Best Use 
 PEER Center Earnings-Based Accountability Explorer  
 Projected pass/fail results under the new rule, filterable by state, institution, program of study, and sector  
 Checking whether a program a student is considering is likely to fail the earnings test  
 PEER Center full data file  
 Program-level underlying data (Appendix D of the report) 
 Deeper analysis for counselors, systems or networks, and researchers  
 College Scorecard  
 Program-level earnings and debt, including earnings four years after graduation and a national median for each field of study 
 Comparing the same field across colleges, and against a national benchmark   
 College Scorecard advisor resources  
 Toolkits for advisors and educators  
 Teaching students to read and use the data  
 A College-by-College Guide to Which Majors Pay Off — or Don’t - The New York Times  
 Median earnings by college program in a compelling data visualization based on data from The HEA Group   
 Helping students understand the range and distribution of earnings within college majors across different postsecondary institutions 
 PSEO Explorer  
 An interactive tool from the US Census that shows job flows and earnings at the state x institution x degree level x general program category (and, for some states, detailed program)  
 Helps to answer what kinds of degrees states and institutions produce, where students with those degrees land in terms of industry, and what they are  
 College warning notices   
 Required alerts when a program is at risk of losing aid, plus Pell lifetime-eligibility notices  
 Red flags to discuss before enrolling or re-enrolling   
 FAFSA low-earnings flag  
 Notice on the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) when a student selects a program that meets Federal Student Aid’s low earning criteria  
 Red flags to discuss before applying, enrolling or re-enrolling   
 Institutions and Programs Really Vary, And That Really Matters  
 The new federal earnings rule has made headlines and caused some handwringing in recent weeks in higher education spaces and the media, but the best available data show that most programs will pass the median earnings standard, and access to Direct Loans for these programs will remain available. 
 Third Way’s Ben Cecil put it succinctly on LinkedIn: “These findings reinforce why the earnings test matters. Most college programs comfortably clear a reasonable baseline for financial value. But students attending programs that don't deserve better protections.” Cecil continues: “At the same time, passing a minimum earnings standard doesn't necessarily mean a program delivers a strong return on investment. We need both: meaningful protections against programs with poor outcomes and better information that helps students understand the value of their college choices.” 
 National College Attainment Network (NCAN) members should continue to reinforce the importance of institutional and program/major selection to students and families. The many available options do not offer the same likelihood of completion or same earnings prospects following completion. Shifting attainment in communities, states, and the nation is going to require that we provide better access opportunities to students but also that the pathways that they are accessing offer the best chance of success. 
 The resources above should be in every NCAN member’s toolkit as resources to inform the advising process. We have never had better publicly available program-level outcomes data than we do now, and hopefully it will continue to improve. Helping students choose not only an institution and a major, but a major at an institution whose instance of that major demonstrates success in the data is a powerful approach to advising. We would love to see more members, and partners across the field, adopt it.
